title: My redeemer liveth (Job 19:25)
hookLine: a flash of hope in the middle of despair
last: I WOULD SPEAK TO THE ALMIGHTY.

lines: CARVE MY WORDS IN THE ROCK.
cards: Chapter nineteen finds Job very low. His brothers are far from him, his friends have forgotten him, his servants treat him like a stranger, and his breath is strange to his own wife.
He begs, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me."
Then a wish: "Oh that my words were now written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book! That with an iron pen and lead they were graven in the rock for ever!"
Carve it in stone, so somebody, someday, knows what happened to me.

teach.b: Then, suddenly: "But as for me, I know that my Redeemer liveth, and that He will witness at the last upon the dust." From the bottom of the pit, I know.

teach.h: GO'EL: THE KINSMAN WHO BUYS BACK.
teach.b: The Hebrew for redeemer is go'el, and it runs through the book of Ruth too: Boaz was the go'el, the kinsman with the right and duty to buy back a family's land and keep a dead man's name alive.
In the Torah, a go'el is the relative who buys back what you lost. So Job, forgotten by everyone, says someone will stand up for me. The text doesn't say who, and readers hear it more than one way.
Some hear God himself, the God Job is arguing with, somehow also his defender.

teach.h: GOD, OR A WITNESS IN HEAVEN?
teach.b: Some connect it to a line a few chapters earlier, "my Witness is in heaven," and hear a defender on Job's side in the heavenly court. Christians read this verse too, and hear it about Jesus.

The lines right after it are hard Hebrew, and translations differ. But the first half stands clear. And notice where it comes: not after his health returns, not after an answer, but in the middle of being forgotten.
Hope here isn't the end of the pain. It's a flash inside it. And Job's wish came true in its own way: his words were written in a book, and people still read them.

how: Jewish readers study Job 19:25 alongside the go'el, the redeeming kinsman of the Torah and the book of Ruth, and God is called redeemer, go'el, in the Tanakh and in daily Jewish prayer.

o: a priest who offers sacrifices for a family
a messenger who brings news from far away
a redeemer, the kinsman who buys back what's lost

games.q: my redeemer liveth — tap the pairs.
p: the go'el in the book of Ruth
Job wants his words in the rock

s: Job says "my redeemer liveth" after his health is restored
he says it while forgotten by brothers and friends.
the same Hebrew word is used for Boaz in the book of Ruth
go'el: the kinsman with the duty to buy back and stand up for family.
the text tells us exactly who Job's redeemer is
it doesn't. readers have heard God, a heavenly witness, and more.

games.q: you're Job. your brothers are far off, your friends have forgotten you, and you've just begged them for pity. what do you say next?
o: that no one will ever stand up for you.
that your redeemer lives and will stand upon the earth.
games.why: "for I know that my redeemer liveth." a flash of hope, right in the middle of despair, before anything has changed.

practice: If something feels heavy right now, let it be there, and inside it look for one small hope: someone who will stand up for you, a morning you're looking forward to, a belief that holds you.
Hold it the way Job held his, not instead of the hard thing but right in the middle of it. If you pray, you can say Job's line, I know that my redeemer liveth.

wordCard.voice: Go'el. Forgotten by his friends, Job says there is a go'el, a redeemer who will stand up for him, alive. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: my redeemer, from go'el, the kinsman who buys back; Job 19:25.

carryVoice: Your line: a flash inside it. Job said I know before anything got better. Until tomorrow.
